passages.happening:
The LORD tells Moses to say to the priests “that a priest is not to defile himself for a dead person among his people” (verse 1). The exceptions are his closest family: mother, father, son, daughter, brother, and an unmarried sister (verses 2-3).

Priests are not to shave bald patches on their heads, trim the edges of their beards or cut their bodies (verse 5). “They must be holy to their God and not profane the name of their God” (verse 6).

A priest is not to marry a woman who has been a prostitute or who has been divorced (verse 7). The people are told, “You are to regard him as holy, since he presents the food of your God” (verse 8). Verse 9 sets a severe penalty for a priest's daughter who becomes a prostitute.
passages.hearers:
Chapters 18 to 20 spoke to all Israel. Now the book turns to the priests, who are held to a stricter rule because of where they serve.

To touch a dead body made a person unclean for a time and unfit to come to the sanctuary. For most people that was a normal part of life. Families prepared and buried their own dead, and it was right that they did. For a priest it meant being kept from his work at the altar. So the law limits it. A priest may bury his nearest relatives, and no one else.

The rule does not forbid a priest to grieve. It keeps the place of the living God apart from death, as the chapters on clean and unclean have done all along.

The shaving and cutting in verse 5 were mourning customs among Israel's neighbors. They were forbidden to all Israel in chapter 19, and the law repeats it for the priests.

A priest's household stood for God before the people. A scandal there dishonored more than one family. That is the thought behind the marriage rules and behind the harsh sentence of verse 9. That verse should be read soberly, as part of the law of ancient Israel. It is no pattern for how any father or any community may treat a daughter today.

The phrase ‘the food of their God’ is an old way of speaking of the offerings. It does not mean that God eats. It pictures the altar as his table and the priests as those who serve at it.
passages.later:
Ezekiel repeats the rule for the priests of a restored temple: “A priest must not defile himself by going near a dead person. However, for a father, a mother, a son, a daughter, a brother, or an unmarried sister, he may do so” (Ezekiel 44:25).

The Gospels show Jesus doing what a priest on duty could not. He took a dead girl by the hand (Mark 5:41), and at the grave of his friend, “Jesus wept” (John 11:35).
passages.asks: The priests had to keep some distance even from grief, because of the work they were given. Ask whether those who serve you in God's name are given room to grieve and to be human. And ask what those who lead owe to the people who watch how they live.

passages.happening:
“The priest who is highest among his brothers, who has had the anointing oil poured on his head and has been ordained to wear the priestly garments, must not let his hair hang loose or tear his garments” (verse 10).

“He must not go near any dead body; he must not defile himself, even for his father or mother” (verse 11). He is not to leave the sanctuary, “for the consecration of the anointing oil of his God is on him” (verse 12).

He is to marry a virgin from his own people (verses 13-14). The passage ends, “for I am the LORD who sanctifies him” (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
The rules grow stricter as they come nearer to the center. The high priest is the one man who goes behind the curtain on the Day of Atonement. More is asked of him than of any other.

He may not make himself unclean even to bury his father or his mother. He may not show the common signs of mourning. The reader has seen this before. On the day Nadab and Abihu died, Aaron was told the same thing (10:6-7). The law now makes it the rule for every high priest after him.

It is a hard demand. The man who carries the people before God has to give up something that everyone else is allowed. The text does not say he feels no grief. It says his office comes first.

And each section of the chapter ends with the same line: ‘I am the LORD who sanctifies’. The priests' holiness is God's gift before it is his demand. They are set apart by him. They do not achieve it.
passages.later:
The letter to the Hebrews describes Jesus in the language of this chapter: he is ‘holy, innocent, undefiled, set apart from sinners’ (Hebrews 7:26).

It adds that this high priest is not far from human weakness: “For we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses” (Hebrews 4:15).
passages.asks: The high priest carried a burden no one else carried. Ask what your calling asks you to lay down that others may keep. And ask whether you pray for those who bear heavy responsibility for others, or mostly judge them.

passages.t: A priest with a physical defect
passages.happening:
The LORD says, “none of your descendants who has a physical defect may approach to offer the food of his God” (verse 17). The list names a man who is blind or lame, who has a broken foot or hand, a curved back, a defect of the eye, a skin complaint or damaged testicles (verses 18-20).

“He may eat the most holy food of his God as well as the holy food, but because he has a defect, he must not go near the veil or approach the altar, so as not to desecrate My sanctuaries. For I am the LORD who sanctifies them” (verses 22-23).

Moses tells all this to Aaron, to his sons and to all the people (verse 24).
passages.hearers:
Modern readers are troubled by this passage, and they are right to be. It needs to be read closely, for what it says and for what it does not say.

It is about one office in one place. It concerns the sons of Aaron who would stand at the altar and go near the veil. It is not about Israelites in general. It shuts no one out of the people of God, or out of worship.

The man is not put out of the priesthood. He remains a priest. He eats the holy food, and even ‘the most holy food’, which only priests could eat. He lives from the altar like his brothers. What he does not do is officiate at it.

The list matches another. The animals offered on the altar had to be ‘without blemish’ (22:17-25), and the list of their defects is very like this one. Most interpreters understand the two together. Everything at the altar, the offering and the one who offered it, was to be a sign of wholeness. The priest's body was part of the picture the sanctuary showed. Some add that royal courts of the ancient world expected the same of those who served in them.

So the rule is about a sign. It is not a judgment of the man. The passage ends by saying that it is the LORD who makes holy.

That does not remove the difficulty, and these notes do not pretend it does. A man born blind, or lamed in an accident, was kept from a work his brothers did. Readers should feel the weight of that.
passages.later:
The prophets looked for a day when those once kept back would be brought in. Through Isaiah God says to eunuchs, who were shut out of the assembly by another law, “I will give them, in My house and within My walls, a memorial and a name better than that of sons and daughters” (Isaiah 56:5).

When Jesus came into the temple, “The blind and the lame came to Him at the temple, and He healed them” (Matthew 21:14). He told his followers whom to ask to their tables: “invite the poor, the crippled, the lame, and the blind” (Luke 14:13).

Paul writes of the church as a body: “the parts of the body that seem to be weaker are indispensable” (1 Corinthians 12:22).
passages.hard:
Does this passage say that a person with a disability is worth less to God?

No. It must never be read that way.

The passage is a rule for who officiated at Israel's altar. It makes no statement about anyone's worth, about anyone's sin, or about how near to God a person may come. The priest it describes ate the holiest food in Israel. And the rest of the Bible speaks plainly. Disability is not punishment for sin, the person's own or anyone else's. Every person, with any disability or illness, is made by God and is precious to him. No one is a mistake.

Readers explain the rule in more than one way. Most take it as a sign, like the unblemished animal: the sanctuary was to show the wholeness of God's presence. Others stress that it belonged to an arrangement that was for a time and pointed beyond itself, and they note the promise of Isaiah 56 and the welcome Jesus gave to the blind and the lame in the temple.

Christians generally hold that in Christ, the one priest whose perfection matters, these limits have been fulfilled, and that disability is no bar to any service in the church. A church that keeps disabled people from its life or its leadership cannot appeal to this chapter.

If you live with chronic illness, pain or disability, you are not a failure of faith. Your worth to God does not rise or fall with your body. If the weight of it is heavy, please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a doctor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: In the temple the blind and the lame came to Jesus, and he received them. Ask who finds it hard to come near in your church: because of steps, noise, pace, or people's looks. And ask what you could change so that they are part of the work, and not only welcomed at the door.
